# Rust on Vehicle Sitting for a Couple of Months

When a vehicle sits stationary for an extended period, such as the two months your car has been parked outside in Ontario since April, surface oxidation is inevitable. The visual evidence you providedâsignificant rust buildup on the front left rotorâconfirms that atmospheric moisture and road salts have taken their toll. However, distinguishing between cosmetic surface rust and structural compromise is the critical first step in your restoration process.

The immediate question is whether to buff out the existing rotors or order new ones. If the rust remains strictly superficial, meaning it has not penetrated deeply into the casting material, mechanical removal is a viable option. The procedure involves removing the wheel assembly, cleaning the hub surface thoroughly with brake cleaner, and then using fine-grit sandpaper (typically starting with 400 grit and moving up to 600 or 800) to scuff the rotor face. This removes the oxidized layer without altering the thickness of the friction material significantly. After sanding, you must wipe the surface clean and apply a light coat of high-temperature brake grease to the hat section where the caliper slides, ensuring the new pads can mount smoothly without sticking.

However, there is a significant trade-off to consider regarding vehicle safety inspections. In Ontario, passing a safety inspection requires not just functional brakes, but often specific clearance on rotor thickness and surface condition. While buffing restores the friction surface, it does not address potential corrosion at the mounting points or within the hat of the rotor. If the rust you see is only on the face, buffing might suffice for immediate functionality. But if the corrosion extends to the wheel studs or the hub flange, the structural integrity is compromised in ways sanding cannot fix.

You mentioned needing to change the bearing hub because it was flagged during your last safety check. This detail changes the equation significantly. If you are replacing the hub assembly anyway, you might as well replace the rotors at that time. Rotors are paired components; if one side has suffered enough exposure to develop heavy rust in two months, the other rotor likely has a similar condition, even if it wasn't visible during your last quick visual check. Replacing them as a pair ensures balanced braking performance and prevents uneven wear on your new hub bearings.

Before you commit to ordering parts, perform a simple test. Spin the rotors by hand while they are mounted. Listen for grinding noises or feel for roughness that isn't smoothed out after a few spins of the brake pedal. If the rotor feels "gritty" under the pads even after cleaning, it indicates pitting rather than just surface rust. In that case, new rotors are mandatory. Trying to buff a pitted rotor is dangerous; the high spots you grind down will dig into your brake pads upon application, leading to vibration and premature wear.

Given that you plan to work on this over the weekend, start by removing the wheels and inspecting the backside of the rotors. Look for rust penetration through the holes where the wheel bolts go. If you see dark stains or flaking metal inside those holes, the rotor must be replaced regardless of how clean the face looks. Once you confirm the extent of the damage, you can make an informed decision on whether to source new rotors or proceed with mechanical refurbishment.

If you decide to replace the components, ensure you order the correct part numbers for your specific vehicle model and year. Mixing old and new rotors in a single axle is generally not recommended due to differences in material hardness and wear patterns. Since you are already tackling the hub bearing replacement, coordinating the rotor installation now will save you from having to return to the shop later just to address brake noise or pulsation.

For those looking for reliable parts sourcing options or advice on specific vehicle models, resources like [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com) can sometimes provide helpful context, though local auto parts stores remain the standard for immediate availability and compatibility verification.
